title: Thalamocortical Loops
intro: No cortical column works alone. Almost every cortical area exchanges signals with a partner nucleus in the thalamus, a structure deep in the forebrain. The thalamus is not just a relay station: it gates what reaches the cortex, and its higher-order nuclei appear to carry messages from one cortical area to another. If your column model has a sensory input stage, you are already modelling a piece of the thalamus, whether you call it that or not.

blocks.text: Intuition: a switchboard with two kinds of wires

Imagine a switchboard (the thalamus) sitting between the outside world and a set of offices (cortical areas). Each line through the switchboard has two kinds of wires. Driver wires carry the actual message: what the retina sees, what the whisker touched. Modulator wires carry no message of their own; they set the volume, open or close the line, and switch it between a faithful 'tonic' mode and an alerting 'burst' mode. Sherman & Guillery's key insight was that the cortex sends both kinds back to the thalamus: L6 sends modulators to the nucleus that feeds it, while L5 sends drivers to higher-order nuclei that pass the message on to other cortical areas.

Sherman & Guillery (1998) distinguished two classes of glutamatergic input by anatomy and physiology. The distinction is useful for modellers because it says which inputs should determine a neuron's receptive field and which should only scale or gate it.

In model terms:  r_out = g(modulators) · f(W_driver · x_driver)

blocks.text: The last line is an idealisation, not a law: real modulators can also shift thresholds and timing. But it captures the important design choice — drivers define what a neuron represents; modulators define how strongly and when it is passed on. The same logic is applied in cortex itself, where feedforward input is often treated as driving and feedback input (via L1 and apical dendrites) as modulatory, though this mapping is debated.
Jones (2001) reviewed a classification of thalamic relay cells into two broad systems, distinguished in primates by calcium-binding proteins.

items: Core cells (parvalbumin-positive in primates): project in a focused, topographic way to the middle layers, especially L4 of primary sensory areas. They carry the precise, point-to-point sensory signal.

Matrix cells (calbindin-positive): project diffusely, across area boundaries, to superficial layers, especially L1, where they contact apical tufts. They are thought to support widespread synchronisation, arousal and the binding of activity across areas.

Most nuclei contain both cell types in different proportions; the classification is a continuum rather than two clean bins. Rodent classifications use different markers but describe similar 'focal versus diffuse' projection patterns.
First-order nuclei relay driver input from subcortical sources to cortex: LGN (retina → V1), VPM/VPL (lemniscal touch → S1), MGBv (inferior colliculus → A1).

Higher-order nuclei receive their driver input from L5 of cortex: pulvinar (visual), POm (somatosensory), MGBd and MGBm (auditory), mediodorsal nucleus (prefrontal). They project to other cortical areas, often higher in the hierarchy.

Both kinds receive modulatory L6 feedback and inhibition from the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), a thin GABAergic shell around the thalamus that is excited by collaterals of both thalamocortical and corticothalamic axons.

blocks.text: The two loops a column takes part in

blocks.source:
1) L6 corticothalamic feedback loop (modulatory, mostly local)

   first-order thalamus ──driver──► L4 ──► ... ──► L6
          ▲      ▲                                  │
          │      └──── TRN (inhibitory) ◄───────────┤
          └───────────── modulator ◄────────────────┘

2) Transthalamic cortico-cortical pathway (driving, between areas)

   area A, L5 (thick-tufted) ──driver──► higher-order thalamus ──► area B (L4/mid layers)
            │                             (pulvinar, POm, ...)
            └── branches also go to brainstem / motor centres

   in parallel:  area A, L2/3 ──direct cortico-cortical──► area B

blocks.text: The L6 loop lets each column adjust the gain and timing of its own input: L6 excitation onto relay cells combined with disynaptic inhibition through TRN can either boost or suppress thalamic responses, depending on timing and firing rates. It has been implicated in sharpening receptive fields, attention-like gating and switching relay cells between tonic and burst firing (relay cells have T-type calcium channels that produce bursts when they are hyperpolarised).

The transthalamic pathway is Sherman & Guillery's more radical proposal: information flows between cortical areas not only through direct cortico-cortical axons but also via L5 → higher-order thalamus → cortex. Because the same L5 axons often branch to motor structures, Guillery & Sherman (2002) suggested that the messages relayed between areas are effectively copies of motor commands (efference copies). This idea is influential and supported by anatomy, but the functional role of the transthalamic route compared with direct cortico-cortical connections is still under active investigation. Hawkins (2021) uses the observation that L5 cells everywhere project to motor-related targets as support for the claim that every column contributes to behaviour.

items: Thalamocortical synapses onto L4 are strong but individually unreliable and depressing; cortex is driven by many synchronous thalamic spikes rather than by single strong inputs (Bruno & Sakmann 2006).

Feedforward inhibition: thalamic input excites L4 PV interneurons as well as excitatory cells, creating a short (a few ms) window during which L4 cells can integrate before being inhibited. This sharpens timing and favours coincident inputs.

Relay cells fire in two modes: tonic (rate roughly proportional to input) and burst (a high-frequency burst of 2–6 spikes after hyperpolarisation, more detectable by cortex). Sherman (2001) proposed bursts act as a 'wake-up call' for novel stimuli; this is a hypothesis.
Loop delays: thalamus → cortex conduction is a few milliseconds in rodents; a full cortex → thalamus → cortex loop is on the order of 10–20 ms. This sets a natural timescale for model feedback.

blocks.text: What this means for your model

items: Your input encoder is a thalamus. Poisson spike trains feeding L4 are a first-order nucleus with no feedback. That is fine to start, but name it so you know what you have left out.

Separate driving and modulatory inputs in code. Give drivers the job of defining receptive fields (and let STDP act on them); make modulators multiplicative gains, threshold shifts or apical-compartment inputs, and generally do not let them create spikes on their own.

Add L6 feedback to the input stage as a cheap gain control: L6 → relay (excitatory, weak, facilitating) plus L6 → TRN-like inhibitory population → relay. This can stabilise input statistics and implement attention-like selection.

For multi-column or hierarchical models, decide whether columns talk directly (L2/3 → L4 of the next area) or through a shared thalamic-like relay driven by L5. The transthalamic option gives you a natural place to inject motor or efference-copy information, which sensorimotor models need (see "Sensorimotor Object Recognition" in section 5).
Matrix-like diffuse input to L1 is a good way to add global context, arousal or a 'mode' signal without retraining feedforward weights.

Use realistic short-term dynamics if timing matters: depressing thalamocortical synapses with strong feedforward inhibition make L4 behave as a coincidence detector, which interacts strongly with STDP.
Remember that thalamic feedback is not yet well understood. Any specific computation you assign to it (prediction, attention, location signals) is a modelling hypothesis — state it as one.
